etymology: Hebrew chetsron, “enclosed” or “surrounded by a wall,” the name of a son of Pharez in the line of Judah; here the man, not the border-town of the south.
biblical_def: Hezron was a son of Pharez (Perez), the son of Judah by Tamar, and he went down into Egypt among the seventy souls of the house of Jacob (Gen 46:12). In the careful register of the chronicler his sons are named: “The sons also of Hezron, that were born unto him; Jerahmeel, and Ram, and Chelubai” (1Chr 2:9). Of these, Ram begat Amminadab, and the line ran on through Nahshon and Salmon and Boaz unto David (Ruth 4:18-22); and from Chelubai, who is Caleb, came another house in Judah. Thus Hezron stands as a hinge in the genealogy, a man little spoken of in his own deeds, yet the channel through which the promise to Judah was carried toward the throne. The Holy Ghost reckoned him worthy to be written, that the generations might be told from Pharez to David, and from David to the Christ (Mat 1:3). It is the glory of the covenant God that He keeps the names of obscure men, threading His purpose of redemption through ordinary households. Hezron did nothing recorded but live and beget, and yet without him the line to the Lamb would be broken. So the LORD ordains the small things and the unnoticed lives to serve His great salvation.
webster_summary: A son of Pharez in the tribe of Judah, father of Ram, Caleb, and Jerahmeel, and an ancestor of David.

etymology: Hebrew karmi, “my vineyard” or “vinedresser,” the name of a man of Judah, father of Achan the troubler; to be distinguished from Carmi the son of Reuben.
biblical_def: Carmi was a man of the tribe of Judah, reckoned in the register through Zerah, and he is remembered chiefly as the father of Achan: “And the sons of Carmi; Achar, the troubler of Israel, who transgressed in the thing accursed” (1Chr 2:7). When the accursed thing was taken at Jericho and the wrath of the LORD kindled against Israel, the man found out by lot was “Achan, the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah” (Josh 7:18). Thus Carmi’s name, which signifies a vineyard, is bound forever to a bitter harvest, for his son brought trouble upon the camp. He must be carefully distinguished from another Carmi, a son of Reuben who came down into Egypt (Gen 46:9). The Scripture is exact in its lineages, and it does not flatter; it tells the worthy descent and the unworthy deed alike. Carmi is named not for any righteousness of his own but as the head of a house through which sin entered the camp of God. The lesson is sober: a man may bear a fruitful name and yet beget a son who troubles Israel, for grace is not inherited as an estate, but each soul must answer to God. Let parents tremble and pray that their seed may fear the LORD.

etymology: Hebrew chamul, “spared” or “pitied,” the name of a son of Pharez in the tribe of Judah, head of the family of the Hamulites.
biblical_def: Hamul was a son of Pharez, the son of Judah, and brother of Hezron: “And the sons of Pharez were Hezron and Hamul” (Gen 46:12). He was among the souls of the house of Jacob that came into Egypt, and from him sprang a family numbered in the wilderness, “of Hamul, the family of the Hamulites” (Num 26:21). The chronicler likewise sets him in the register: “The sons of Pharez; Hezron, and Hamul” (1Chr 2:5). His name signifies “spared” or “pitied,” a fitting word for a son of that tribe through whom the LORD would show His mercy to all the families of the earth. Hamul did no recorded deed; he is a name and a family and no more. Yet the Spirit reckoned him worthy to be written, that the seed of Pharez might be told and the tribe of Judah numbered before the LORD. There is a quiet dignity in such a name: a man spared, a household kept, a family carried on. The God who pitied and spared a son of Judah is the God whose tender mercies are over all His works, and who has compassion on those He has chosen. Hamul reminds us that to be remembered by God, and spared in His mercy, is a greater thing than to be famous among men.

etymology: Hebrew zerach, “rising” or “dawning,” as of the light; the name of a son of Judah by Tamar, twin of Pharez; to be distinguished from Zerah the Ethiopian and Zerah of Edom.
biblical_def: Zerah was a son of Judah by Tamar, the twin brother of Pharez, born after a strange travail wherein his hand came forth first and was bound with a scarlet thread, and then drew back that his brother might be born before him: “And afterward came out his brother, that had the scarlet thread upon his hand: and his name was called Zarah” (Gen 38:30). His name, signifying a “rising” or “dawning” of light, recalls the brightness of that scarlet token. The chronicler sets him in the register of Judah and names his sons: “and the sons of Zerah; Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara: five of them in all” (1Chr 2:6). From this house came the wise men whom Solomon’s wisdom excelled, the Ezrahites of song and proverb. He must be distinguished from Zerah the Ethiopian who came against Asa (2Chr 14:9), and from Zerah a duke of Edom (Gen 36:17). Zerah was not the chosen line of the throne, for that ran through Pharez his brother; yet the LORD did not forget him, but gave to his seed a portion of wisdom and of psalmody. So God distributes His gifts as He will, that no house of His people might be wholly without honour, and that the praise might redound to the Giver and not to the gifted.
webster_summary: A son of Judah by Tamar, twin brother of Pharez, whose hand drew back at the birth and from whom sprang the Ezrahite sages.

etymology: Hebrew ’ethan, “perpetual,” “enduring,” or “firm”; with ezrachi, “the Ezrahite,” of the line of Zerah son of Judah.
biblical_def: Ethan the Ezrahite was a wise man of the line of Zerah, the son of Judah, numbered among the sons of Zerah: “Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara” (1Chr 2:6). His renown for wisdom was so great that the Holy Ghost set it as a measure of Solomon’s surpassing gift: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol” (1Ki 4:31). To his name is ascribed the eighty-ninth Psalm, “Maschil of Ethan the Ezrahite,” a great song that pleads the covenant made with David and laments the affliction of the LORD’s anointed, yet clings to the sure mercies sworn in truth. His name, signifying “perpetual” or “enduring,” befits a man whose psalm rests upon the everlasting covenant: “Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations” (Psa 89:4). Yet for all his wisdom, Ethan was excelled, that the glory might go to the wisdom of God set forth in Solomon, and supremely in Christ, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom (Col 2:3). Here is the doctrine: the wisest of men is but a candle before the noonday Sun. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Pro 9:10), and the wisdom of God is wiser than the wisest of men (1Co 1:25).

etymology: Hebrew heman, “faithful” or “trusty”; with ezrachi, “the Ezrahite,” of the line of Zerah son of Judah.
biblical_def: Heman the Ezrahite was a wise man of the line of Zerah, the son of Judah, numbered among the sons of Zerah: “Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara” (1Chr 2:6). His wisdom, with Ethan’s, was set as a measure against which Solomon’s surpassing gift was reckoned: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda” (1Ki 4:31). To his name is ascribed the eighty-eighth Psalm, “A Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite,” the darkest of all the songs, a cry from the lowest pit wherein the soul is full of troubles and the eye mourneth by reason of affliction, yet still it cries unto the LORD by day and by night. He must be carefully distinguished from Heman the Levite, the grandson of Samuel, who was a singer set over the service of song in the house of the LORD (1Chr 6:33); this Heman is the Ezrahite of Judah’s line. His name signifies “faithful,” and faithful indeed is the soul that, sunk in deepest darkness, will not let go its God. Here is the doctrine of a tried faith: it may walk in darkness and have no light, yet it stays itself upon the LORD (Isa 50:10). And here too is the wisdom of God, which excelled this sage, that men might trust not in the wise but in the Wisdom of God Himself, even Christ crucified.

etymology: Hebrew kalkol, “sustenance” or “nourishment,” the name of a son of Zerah, a wise man of Judah’s line; written Chalcol in the book of Kings.
biblical_def: Calcol was a son of Zerah, the son of Judah, numbered among the wise men of that house: “And the sons of Zerah; Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara” (1Chr 2:6). His wisdom, with that of his brethren, was set as a measure of the surpassing gift granted to Solomon: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol” (1Ki 4:31). There the name is written Chalcol, and the sages are called “the sons of Mahol,” that is, sons of the dance or of song, a household renowned for wisdom and psalmody in Israel before the days of the king. His name signifies “sustenance” or “nourishment,” and it is the LORD who nourisheth the soul of the wise. Calcol himself did no recorded deed; he is named only that the wisdom of Solomon might be magnified above the wisest of his nation, and through Solomon the wisdom of God that was greater than Solomon (Mat 12:42). Here is the lesson: the renown of the godly sage, however great, is but a stepping-stone whereby Scripture lifts our eyes to a greater Wisdom. The wisest men of the earth are gathered up only to be excelled, that the praise might go to Him in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

etymology: Hebrew dara’, perhaps “pearl of wisdom” or “bearer of knowledge”; a son of Zerah of Judah, written Darda in the book of Kings.
biblical_def: Dara was a son of Zerah, the son of Judah, named last among the five sons of that house: “Zimri, and Ethan, and Heman, and Calcol, and Dara: five of them in all” (1Chr 2:6). In the book of Kings his name appears as Darda among the wise men whom Solomon excelled: “For he was wiser than all men; than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol” (1Ki 4:31). Thus Dara and Darda are one, the slight difference of letters being no stranger thing than is common between the registers and the histories. His name has been understood to signify a “pearl of wisdom” or a “bearer of knowledge,” fitting for one numbered among the sages of his people. Dara did no recorded deed, spoke no recorded word; he is a name in a line and a wise man in a list. Yet the Holy Ghost reckoned him worthy to be written, that the wisdom of Solomon might be magnified, and the wisdom of God beyond Solomon. Here is a quiet rebuke to the pride of learning: a man may be among the wisest in all the earth and leave behind only his name. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Pro 9:10), and that wisdom, laid up in Christ, alone endures when the renown of sages is forgotten and their very names are doubled in the telling.

corruption_paragraphs: Dara is a name set in the register of Judah, and no movement of the present age has troubled itself to redefine him. The dictionary records him that the reader who meets the name among the sons of Zerah may know that Dara of the Chronicles is Darda of the Kings, one wise man under two spellings.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom (Pro 9:10). Dara was among the wisest in the earth, yet left behind only his name; the wisdom that endures is hid in Christ (Col 2:3), and the praise belongs to God.

etymology: Hebrew ’akar, “to trouble” or “to bring disaster”; a son of Carmi of Judah, called Achan in Joshua, Achar in the Chronicles, the troubler of Israel.
biblical_def: Achar, who is Achan, was a son of Carmi of the tribe of Judah, in the line of Zerah, and his name is bound forever to the sin of the camp at Jericho: “And the sons of Carmi; Achar, the troubler of Israel, who transgressed in the thing accursed” (1Chr 2:7). When Jericho fell, the LORD had commanded that the city and all therein be devoted and accursed, and that none should take of the spoil. But Achan coveted and took a goodly Babylonish garment, two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold, and hid them in his tent; and the anger of the LORD was kindled against all Israel, so that they fled before the men of Ai (Josh 7:1). This was sin in the camp: the secret transgression of one man brought defeat and death upon the whole congregation, for Israel was a covenant body and not a heap of severed souls. By lot the LORD found him out, and Joshua said, “Why hast thou troubled us? the LORD shall trouble thee this day. And all Israel stoned him with stones” (Josh 7:25). They raised over him a great heap of stones in the valley, which was called the valley of Achor, that is, of trouble, unto this day (Josh 7:26). Here is the doctrine plainly: sin is no private matter, covetousness is idolatry, and the holiness of God will not wink at the accursed thing hidden in the tent. Yet the valley of trouble becomes a door of hope to the penitent (Hos 2:15), for the blood of Christ alone cleanseth the camp.
webster_summary: A son of Carmi of Judah, the troubler of Israel, who took of the accursed thing at Jericho and was stoned in the valley of Achor.

He was stoned in the valley of Achor, named for the trouble he wrought.

corruption_summary: A man whose sin is named plainly in Scripture: covetousness is idolatry, and the hidden accursed thing brings trouble upon the whole camp of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Achar is no contested doctrine but a warning written in blood. His sin was real sin: he coveted the accursed thing, took it, and hid it in his tent, and the wrath of God fell upon all Israel. The Scripture does not soften it nor make it a misfortune; it names it transgression in the thing accursed (Josh 7:1), and it shows that the secret sin of one defiles the whole body.

The principle to recover is the holiness of God who will not wink at hidden sin, and the covenant solidarity of His people, wherein the camp is troubled by the transgressor in its midst. Covetousness is idolatry (Col 3:5), and no goodly garment nor wedge of gold is worth the trouble it brings. Yet the valley of Achor is made a door of hope (Hos 2:15) to the penitent, for the blood of Christ alone purges the accursed thing and cleanses the camp of God.
roots_summary: From the Hebrew ’akar, “to trouble,” Achar names the troubler of Israel who took the accursed thing.

etymology: Hebrew racham, “mercy,” “compassion,” or “tender love”; the name of a man in the Calebite line of the tribe of Judah.
biblical_def: Raham was a man of the tribe of Judah, set in the register of the house of Caleb: “And the sons of Shema; Raham, the father of Jorkoam: and Rekem begat Shammai” (1Chr 2:44). He was the son of Shema and the father of Jorkoam, a link in that Calebite branch which the chronicler traces among the families of Judah after the return from captivity, when the names of the fathers were sought out and written down. Raham did no recorded deed and spoke no recorded word; he is a name only, and the father of a name. Yet his name is rich, for racham signifies “mercy” and “tender compassion,” the very bowels of pity, the word by which the LORD reveals Himself as “merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy” (Psa 103:8). It is a fitting thing that in the long and dry lists of Judah’s households there should stand a man whose very name is Mercy. For these registers are not idle; they are the LORD’s remembrance of His people, the proof that He forgets none of those that are His. He who numbered Raham and his son in the tribe of the Lion numbers also the hairs of His children’s heads. Here is comfort: the obscure believer, who leaves behind only a name in a forgotten list, is yet held in the tender mercy of God, written in a better register, the Lamb’s book of life.
webster_summary: A man of the Calebite line of Judah, son of Shema and father of Jorkoam, whose name signifies mercy.
